item.research_question: How does the addition of B4C and the variation of starting particle sizes of solvent (TaC) versus solute (HfC, Mo2C, TiC) carbides influence the phase evolution, crystal structure transformation, and mechanical properties of refractory high-entropy ceramic composites synthesized via pulsed current processing?
item.material_system: Quaternary (HfC, Mo2C, TaC, TiC) and Quinary (HfC, Mo2C, TaC, TiC, B4C) high-entropy carbide composites
item.processing_route: Pulsed current processing (Spark Plasma Sintering) at 1800 °C for 5 min under vacuum with a uniaxial pressure of 60 MPa and a heating rate of 100 °C/min
item.test_conditions: Microstructure and phase identification via SEM (15 kV), EDS, and XRD (5–120° 2 Theta); nanohardness measured with a Berkovich indenter at 100 mN load and ambient temperature
key_findings: The quaternary (4-HEC) composite formed two FCC phases: a Ta-rich phase (0.4429 nm) and a high-entropy phase (0.4399 nm) with a hardness of 28.4 GPa.
Adding B4C induced a transformation from FCC to a hexagonal structure in the high-entropy phase with higher solute content (HEC2), while a lower-content phase (HEC1) retained the FCC structure.
The addition of B4C delayed the sintering shrinkage temperature range from 1000–1600 °C (4-HEC) to 1370–1690 °C (5-HEC), indicating hindered atomic diffusion.
Reducing the particle size of solute carbides (HfC, Mo2C, TiC) promoted interdiffusion, resulting in a higher fraction of the hexagonal structured HEC phase compared to using larger particles.
Tuning the particle size of the solvent carbide (TaC) had a negligible effect on the final phase composition.
Reducing TaC particle size from −325 mesh to <1 µm increased the nanohardness of the composite from 21.4 GPa to 23.1 GPa.
The HEC(fine) composite (finest solute particles) showed a Young's modulus of 401 GPa, an improvement over the 380.7 GPa observed in the HEC(+) composite.
item.mechanism: TaC acts as the solvent carbide due to its low metal vacancy formation energy; constituent atoms diffuse into TaC vacancies causing lattice distortion. The addition of B4C promotes the diffusion of B atoms, which have longer bond lengths than C atoms, inducing severe lattice distortion that transforms the FCC structure to hexagonal. Reducing solute particle size shortens diffusion distances, enhancing the kinetics of phase transformation toward the hexagonal structure.
item.limitations: The study notes that EDS lacks accuracy for quantitative analysis of light elements, and the presence of porosity in some samples complicated the nanoindentation testing, requiring matrix indentations to obtain bulk property averages.
item.future_work: The authors state that a detailed investigation on the sintering behavior of ceramic precursors to form high-entropy ceramic composites will be reported later, elsewhere.
quotes: The high entropy phase and Ta-rich phase displayed a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure with similar lattice parameters, suggesting that TaC acted as a solvent carbide during phase evolution.
With the increase in the number of principal elements, on the addition of B4C, the crystal structure of the HEC phase transformed from FCC to a hexagonal structure.

Reducing the size of solute carbide components HfC, Mo2C, and TiC could effectively promote the interdiffusion process, resulting in a higher fraction of a hexagonal structured HEC phase in the material.
